title: Warning your contacts without spreading panic
body_md:
## A warning has to land before the payment does

Somewhere an aunt is looking at a message that seems to come from you: a donation appeal, a payment link, her thumb already near the button. You did not write it, and she has no way to know that. The people who received requests in your name need a warning they can act on. They do not need the technical details, and they do not need you to beat yourself up in public. What helps is four plain facts: which channel was affected, roughly when, what kind of request went out, and the safe thing to do now. If you do not yet know how far it reaches, say so, and update the warning when you do.

### Pick the audience by who was actually exposed

Start with anyone who received a suspicious message, was asked to pay, shared information, or might open an attachment. Reach them directly and quickly, even while recovery is still going on, if a harmful request is circulating. A wider message can help when you cannot tell who received what. A public notice is sometimes right for an account many people use, but it can draw “recovery” pitches from strangers and give away more personal detail than you meant to. No rule forbids a public post or an email once the account is secured; choose the route that reliably reaches the people affected.

Where you can, prove it is you through a channel the recipient already knows: a number saved in their phone, a conversation in person, a separate work channel. If the compromised email is your only route, tell people how to check your warning on their own. Leave out the malicious link, and do not forward the original message as an example. If someone needs it to file a report, ask them to keep it to themselves rather than pass it on.

### What goes on the notice

Think of the paper taped inside an elevator: what broke, since roughly when, what to do instead, when there will be news. A short version: “Messages from my [account/channel] between [approximate dates] may have included a payment or login request I did not send. Please do not use its links or pay. If you acted on it, contact your bank or the relevant account provider promptly, and reach me on the number you already have. I will update this if the affected window changes.” Adapt the action to what actually happened, and do not promise that every message is safe now until you have regained control.

If coworkers’ information or systems may be involved, coordinate the notice with your organization’s security team, which may have required procedures. Keep a short list of whom you warned and what they reported, so you can follow up with each of them, without copying your whole address book into a file an attacker could find.

widget_config.goal: Send a calm, targeted warning that says what is still uncertain, stops people acting on a forged request, and offers a way to verify you.
widget_config.today_action: Draft a two-sentence warning for an invented compromised account whose time window you do not know. Save it as a template, not as a message to send.
widget_config.scope: General advice on talking to people you know. Your employer may have separate notification duties, and local law may apply to data breaches. The people in the examples are invented.

blocks.title: A fake invoice from a real inbox
blocks.situation: While an intruder was signed in to Ilya’s email, three coworkers received a fake invoice from him. One of them says the payment is still pending.
blocks.analysis: Ilya phones that coworker at once on a number he already has, asks them to stop the payment and call their bank, and only then warns the others, giving the affected window and a way to check that the warning is really his. He coordinates the work contacts with IT.

blocks.title: A newsletter right on schedule
blocks.situation: Rosa’s friend sends a newsletter every week at the same hour, and this week’s arrives on time. The friend’s account, though, was compromised not long ago.
blocks.analysis: It may well be genuine. Rosa asks through the separate channel the two of them usually use, and the friend confirms the send was scheduled. A good warning describes the suspicious requests; it does not paint every ordinary message as malicious.

blocks.title: Four relatives and one fake appeal
blocks.setup: An invented family scare: your messaging account sent a fake donation request to four relatives. You have your access back, but you do not yet know when it began.

choices.text: The four relatives directly, beginning with anyone who might be about to pay.
choices.consequence: The live risk is dealt with quickly.
choices.explanation: Do not wait for a perfect picture of the scope while a payment may be in flight.

choices.text: A post on your public feed, so everyone sees it at once.
choices.consequence: The relatives who actually got the message may never see it.
choices.explanation: Your audience is whoever was actually exposed.

choices.text: Only the chat that was compromised: a quick line, no explanation.
choices.consequence: They may doubt the warning, or miss it.
choices.explanation: Give people an independent way to check that it is you.

choices.text: A number they already know, or another established channel. If only the hijacked chat works, say how to check it is you.
choices.consequence: The recipients can tell the warning is really yours.
choices.explanation: A channel they already know lets them check you without trusting the hijacked one.

steps.prompt: What do you tell people about timing?

choices.text: Say you know the exact minute it began.
choices.consequence: Someone may wrongly dismiss an earlier request.
choices.explanation: Precision you cannot back up does harm.

choices.text: Give the approximate window you know, and promise to update it if it changes.
choices.consequence: The uncertainty stays visible and the warning goes out without delay.
choices.explanation: Never invent an exact start time.

steps.prompt: A relative has already paid. What instruction helps?

choices.text: Tell them to contact their bank or payment provider promptly and keep a private copy of the request.
choices.consequence: They can start their own recovery.
choices.explanation: Do not promise reimbursement, and do not ask them to send you sensitive details.

choices.text: Send the scam link around the whole family as proof.
choices.explanation: Describe the pattern; do not spread the lure.

blocks.debrief: Warn the people you know were reached, quickly and accurately, by a route they trust, and give them one thing to do. Retry any decision you would like to see play out differently, then run the whole sequence again.

questions.prompt: The account is still locked and messages are going out. Must you wait until recovery is finished before warning anyone?

choices.text: Yes, a warning is only useful afterwards.
choices.explanation: Recipients may act in the meantime.

choices.text: No. Warn the people affected now, through a separate trusted route.
choices.explanation: The first goal is to stop anyone acting on the fake request.

questions.prompt: Which detail belongs in a warning to recipients?

choices.text: A description of the fake request, and what to do if they acted on it.
choices.explanation: It lets them judge their own risk and respond.

choices.text: Your recovery codes and your full account history.
choices.explanation: Those add risk and do nothing for them.

questions.prompt: A recipient asks whether an ordinary-looking message was genuine. What is the best answer?

choices.text: Check your records and confirm, or say you are unsure and verify it separately.
choices.explanation: Do not claim more than you have established.

choices.text: Call every message from the past month fraudulent.
choices.explanation: That misleads people and causes needless disruption.
